sections.title: 1. Tests for frontal and parietal lobes

blocks.title: Bedside tests of frontal lobe function
rows: Comparing two objects tests 'categorisation' (not a description of common 'parts'); a test of abstract ability

Naming supermarket items or animals (category fluency), or words starting with given letters (**FAS**, word fluency); tests speed, accuracy and the ability to shift from one set of objects to the next (supermarket list must include fruits, baked goods, drinks, cleaning items etc.)
Fist-palm-edge, must not be verbally facilitated; tests motor planning, execution and error correction
Tests response inhibition, absence of perseveration and resistance to interference
e.g. 'How tall is an average English woman?'; needs abstract, not mere factual, thinking

Part A: simple number sequence joins the dots; Part B alternates numbers and letters and is thought more sensitive to frontal lobe dysfunction. Not specific for frontal lobe - tests visuomotor tracing, attention, conceptualisation and set shifting
Alternate pyramids and squares drawing, proverb interpretation, and to some extent frontal release signs and digit span (normal 7+/-2 forwards, 5+/-1 backwards) reflect frontal functions

blocks.mnemonic: Some Lazy Lions Grab Cold Tea

blocks.title: Bedside tests of parietal lobe function
rows: Ability to draw shapes and construct geometrical patterns is a parietal (esp. non-dominant) function

Dominant parietal damage can cause finger agnosia (part of Gerstmann syndrome); test = correctly show index, middle and ring fingers. Interlocking fingers test (copy examiner's interlocked fingers) is also a parietal test
Dominant parietal damage can cause acalculia (part of Gerstmann syndrome); tests simple mathematical functions. Mere recognition and use of numbers is arithmetic ability, which is often intact
Recognising a number or letter scratched on the skin without seeing; bilateral parietal function (somatosensory cortices)
Dominant parietal damage can cause right-left disorientation (part of Gerstmann syndrome); test = touch right ear lobe with left index finger with eyes closed
Recognising objects by palpation without visual inspection; bilateral parietal function (somatosensory cortices)
Cortical sensation; bilateral somatosensory cortical function
Hemineglect is a feature of parietal lesions; letter or star cancellation, line bisection, draw-a-person or draw-a-tree tasks identify hemineglect

blocks.text: Copying intersecting pentagons is the task a non-dominant parietal lesion makes hardest - it tests constructional praxis. The explanation lists visuospatial dysfunction, topographical memory loss and constructional/dressing apraxia as non-dominant parietal effects (seen with either hemisphere, but more often and more severe on the non-dominant side); reading, writing a sentence, serial 7s and stating location are the distractors.

**Q1**: a man leaves food on one side of his plate and bisects a line nearer its right end - the lesion is the right parietal lobe (neglect of personal and extrapersonal space is usually a right hemisphere lesion, often inferior parietal or prefrontal).

**Q5**: response inhibition is specifically tested by the Go-No-Go test (tap once for one tap, withhold for two taps), not by category fluency, cognitive estimates, digit span or proverbs; impulsivity reflects failure of response inhibition seen in inferior frontal pathology.
**Q38**: the ability to recognise a number or letter scratched on the skin without seeing is graphesthesia (a parietal lobe function), not stereognosis or 2-point discrimination.

**Q12**: Benton verbal fluency test is the frontal lobe test; the explanation lists verbal fluency, category tests, trail making, Wisconsin card sorting and Stroop as frontal tests, and puts Benton visual retention, speech sound perception, Seashore rhythms and revised Wechsler memory scale under temporal lobe tests; Rey-Osterrieth complex figure is not a frontal test.

The California Verbal Learning Test is the '**NOT** a frontal lobe test' answer: the explanation lists the frontal tests (Stroop, Halstead trail making, cognitive estimates, Tower of London, **WCST**, verbal fluency, Luria's motor tests, multiple errands) and says the **CVLT** assesses verbal memory - it may be affected in frontal lesions but is not a specific frontal test.

Naming as many animals as possible in one minute is category fluency, a frontal lobe test of lexical fluency - it tests speed, accuracy and the ability to shift from a narrow set to the next; temporal, parietal, occipital and cerebellar are the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Temporal-lobe test list from the question bank
blocks.note: Notes do not classify Benton visual retention, speech sound perception, Seashore rhythms or **WMS-R** as temporal lobe tests (notes describe Benton as a short-term visual memory test, Halstead-Reitan includes speech-sounds and rhythm tests). **Q12**'s explanation assigns them to the temporal lobe - not stated in the notes.

blocks.subtopic: Animal models of depression: forced swim test
blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q2**: the forced swim (behavioural despair/Porsolt) test measures the effect of antidepressants in laboratory animals: after an initial 15 minutes of swimming and a repeat 5-minute session a day later, the time with no effort to escape (immobility time) indexes helplessness and is decreased by antidepressants.

Not in the notes. Raclopride is a **D2** antagonist that can be radiolabelled with carbon-11 for **PET** to assess the distribution of **D2** receptors and the degree of endogenous dopamine binding (keyed answer: **D2** receptors).

bullets.text: Frontal tests: similarities (abstraction), lexical/category fluency (speed and set-shifting), Luria motor test, go/no-go (response inhibition), cognitive estimates, trail making B.
Trail Making B (alternating numbers/letters) is more sensitive to frontal dysfunction but not specific - also tests visuomotor tracing, attention, set shifting.
Digit span normal 7+/-2 forwards, 5+/-1 backwards; frontal release signs and digit span reflect frontal function to some extent.
Parietal tests: copying shapes (non-dominant), finger identification, calculation, right-left orientation (dominant parietal = Gerstmann elements).
Graphesthesia, stereognosis and two-point discrimination are bilateral parietal somatosensory cortex functions.
Hemineglect (parietal): letter/star cancellation, line bisection, draw-a-person/tree.
CVLT is not a frontal test (verbal memory); animal-naming = frontal category fluency.
Intersecting-pentagon copying fails in non-dominant parietal lesions (constructional praxis).

blocks.title: Frontal lobe lesions
rows: Slight elevation of mood, increased talkativeness, tendency to joke inappropriately (Witzelsucht)
Frontal release signs (grasp and suck reflexes)
Decomposition of gait and sphincter incontinence
Motor speech disorder with agraphia, with or without oro-buccal apraxia (left)
Varying combinations of grasping, sucking, obligate imitative movements, utilization behavior
Loss of verbal fluency with perseveration (left)

blocks.text: Specific frontal syndromes named in the notes: pseudo depressive, dysexecutive and pseudo psychopathic.
Gelastic seizure: an epileptic fit of incessant 'laughter', not necessarily euphoria; it occurs with left prefrontal seizures.

blocks.subtopic: Localisation of the specific frontal syndromes
blocks.note: Notes name pseudodepressive, dysexecutive and pseudopsychopathic syndromes but do not localise them. **Q46**'s explanation: **DLPFC** lesions give dysexecutive syndrome (poor planning, judgment, insight, concrete inflexible attitude, reduced spontaneous behaviour); orbitofrontal lesions give pseudopsychopathic syndrome (poor impulse control, explosive outbursts); **Q8** links ventromedial frontal lesions to pseudodepressive syndrome (apathy).

blocks.text: Dorsolateral prefrontal syndrome = poor planning ability (dysexecutive syndrome: diminished judgement, planning and insight, concrete inflexible attitude, reduced spontaneous behaviour) - **NOT** poor impulse control or psychopathic dyscontrol, which the explanation assigns to orbitofrontal lesions (pseudopsychopathic syndrome).

Olfactory disturbance is keyed as a localising sign for frontal lesions, but the explanation warns that anosmia is itself not a good localising sign because the cause is often peripheral (nostrils); the classic frontal presentation it names is olfactory groove meningioma - anosmia, loss of inhibition, memory impairment, headaches and visual symptoms.

Reduced verbal fluency, loss of insight and a silly jocular affect (with mild aphasia, wandering and preserved motor function) point to frontal lesions - the keyed scan finding is bilateral frontal atrophy, not occipito-parietal or diffuse atrophy.

items.text: Lesion of ventromedial frontal cortex is associated with apathy; the explanation says this results in pseudodepressive syndrome.
Loss of verbal fluency = left frontal lesion; motor speech disorder is a feature of left frontal lesions due to damage to Broca's area.
Forced utilization behaviour is keyed to the orbitofrontal lobe (damage to orbital frontal structures and caudate nuclei).

Bilateral orbito-frontal contre-coup injury is the **MRI** finding for behaviour change, violent outbursts, impulsivity and reduced fluency after head injury; pseudopsychopathy is a result of orbitofrontal damage.
Anosmia is not a good localising sign for frontal lesions - the cause is often peripheral (nostrils).

blocks.title: Parietal lobe lesions
rows: Spatial disorientation and visual spatial defects
Bilateral ideomotor and ideational apraxia (more prominent with left-sided lesions)
Homonymous hemianopia or inferior quadrantanopia (incongruent or congruent)
Tactile agnosia (bimanual astereognosis) (more prominent with left-sided lesions)
Neglect of the opposite side of external space (right parietal lesions)
Anosognosia, dressing and constructional apraxias (may occur with lesions of either hemisphere; more frequent and severe with non-dominant right lesions)
Gerstmann syndrome (dysgraphia, dyscalculia, finger agnosia, right-left confusion) (left)

blocks.mnemonic: FALW: Finger agnosia, Acalculia, Left-right confusion, Writing (agraphia)

blocks.text: Hemi-neglect is the '**NOT** a feature of Gerstmann syndrome' answer - the dominant parietal tetrad is finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, dysgraphia/agraphia and dyscalculia/acalculia.

Gerstmann syndrome = dominant parietal lobe signs (damage to the inferior parietal lobule of the dominant hemisphere); aphasia, hemineglect, cortical blindness and dressing apraxia are the distractors.

blocks.title: Temporal lobe lesions
rows: Auditory, visual, olfactory and gustatory hallucinations
Varying degrees of amusia and/or visual agnosia
Hypermetamorphopsia (compulsion to attend to all visual stimuli), hyperorality, hypersexuality, blunted emotional reactivity (Kluver-Bucy syndrome; the full syndrome is rarely seen)

blocks.title: Psychopathology of the auras of temporal lobe epilepsy
rows: Most common of auras, causing epigastric aura, salivation, sometimes vertigo etc.
Compulsion to think on a certain restricted topic
Intrusion of stereotyped words or thoughts
Recall of expansive memories in incredible detail, as if running a video show of the past
Isolated auras with hallucinations, depersonalisations, micropsia or macropsia, deja vu or jamais vu (especially if right-sided origin)
Hallucinations of taste and smell associated with dream-like reminiscence and altered consciousness

blocks.text: Aura is keyed to complex partial seizures (particularly temporal lobe complex partial epilepsy), not grand mal, petit mal or myoclonic seizures; auras are brief (seconds) and stereotyped - e.g. autonomic/visceral (epigastric), depersonalisation, derealisation, affective change, illusions and hallucinations.

Epileptic automatisms last a few seconds to minutes (stereotyped gesturing, grasping, lip-smacking, chewing), with subsequent amnesia; only very occasionally are they prolonged (fugue states) - not hours, days or months.

A sensory aura of tingling, numbness, vague pain, body-image distortion, vertigo and visual illusions localises the focus to the parietal lobe; pain is rare as an epileptic phenomenon overall, but one-quarter of parietal lobe seizures have pain as a prominent symptom.

Geschwind syndrome: an uncommon type of personality change reported in epilepsy patients (esp. **TLE**); symptoms include hypergraphia, circumstantiality, interpersonal viscosity, hyperreligiosity and hyposexuality. It is thought to result from lost connectivity among cerebral areas, which may also explain the personality features often seen in epilepsy (increased suspiciousness and paranoia).

**Q48**: increased oral and sexual behaviour, placidity, loss of fear or anger and apathy = Kluver-Bucy syndrome (bilateral temporal lobe ablation involving uncus, amygdala and hippocampus; in humans seen in Alzheimer's, Pick's, herpes simplex encephalitis and tumours with medial temporal involvement).

blocks.note: Notes list amusia under unilateral temporal lesions without side. **Q17**: reduced Seashore Musical Aptitude Test score and receptive amusia are keyed to right temporal damage - not stated in the notes.

blocks.title: Occipital lobe lesions
rows: Contralateral (congruent) homonymous hemianopia, central (splitting the macula) or peripheral; also homonymous hemiachromatopsia
Elementary (unformed) hallucinations - usually due to irritative lesions
Anton syndrome (visual anosognosia, denial of cortical blindness)
If deep white matter or splenium of corpus callosum involved: alexia and colour-naming defect
Visual illusions (metamorphopsias) and hallucinations (more frequent with right-sided lesions)

blocks.text: **Q3**: loss of body-part identification plus inability to calculate after **TBI** = left angular gyrus (Gerstmann syndrome: dominant angular and supramarginal gyri).

**Q15**: Gerstmann syndrome = dominant parietal lobe (finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, dyscalculia); non-dominant parietal lesions give anosognosia, hemisomatognosia, dressing apraxia and prosopagnosia.

**Q23**: in a right-sided brain lesion the most likely deficit is visuospatial neglect; visuospatial disorders, dressing and constructional apraxias and anosognosia occur with either hemisphere but are more frequent and severe with non-dominant lesions.

bullets.text: Frontal unilateral: contralateral spastic hemiplegia, mild mood elevation/Witzelsucht, release signs, anosmia; left side: motor speech disorder with agraphia and loss of verbal fluency with perseveration.
Frontal bilateral: pseudobulbar palsy, abulia, gait decomposition with sphincter incontinence, grasping/sucking/utilization behaviour.
Gelastic seizure (incessant laughter, not necessarily euphoria) occurs with left prefrontal seizures.
Parietal unilateral: corticosensory syndrome/extinction, neglect (right), Gerstmann (left); bilateral: Balint, anosognosia, dressing and constructional apraxias, tactile agnosia.
Temporal bilateral: hallucinations in all modalities, dreamy states, Korsakoff defect, apathy/placidity, Kluver-Bucy (hypermetamorphopsia, hyperorality, hypersexuality).
Geschwind syndrome in TLE: hypergraphia, circumstantiality, viscosity, hyperreligiosity, hyposexuality.
Occipital bilateral: cortical blindness (pupils reactive), Anton syndrome, achromatopsia, prosopagnosia, Balint; unilateral: contralateral homonymous hemianopia, formed-object agnosia.
DLPFC = poor planning (dysexecutive); orbitofrontal = poor impulse control (pseudopsychopathic).
Auras are most common in temporal lobe complex partial seizures; automatisms last seconds to minutes.

facts.label: Geschwind syndrome
facts.value: Hypergraphia, circumstantiality, interpersonal viscosity, hyperreligiosity, hyposexuality

blocks.text: **WAIS**: the most widely used intelligence test in clinical practice. The latest revision, **WAIS-III**, is for persons 16 to 89 years; **WISC-III** is used for under 16; **WPPSI-R** for ages 4 to 6.5 years. **WAIS** has 11 subtests (six verbal, five performance) yielding verbal **IQ**, performance **IQ** and full-scale **IQ**.

'All but' trap: digit span is a **VERBAL** **WAIS** subtest, so it is the answer to 'performance subtests include all but'. Performance = picture arrangement, block design, picture completion, digit symbol, matrix reasoning; verbal = similarities, arithmetic, digit span, vocabulary, information, comprehension.
Digit symbol is the non-verbal (performance) **WAIS** test; digit span, vocabulary, arithmetic and information are all verbal subtests.

Information is the **WAIS** test resistant to brain damage - hold tests are vocabulary, information, object assembly and picture completion; non-hold tests are block design, digit span, similarities and digit symbol. The explanation adds that the hold/non-hold resistance idea is 'disputed'.

Picture completion is keyed as the **WAIS** part most resistant to brain damage: hold tests reflect old knowledge, whereas no-hold tests (digit symbol, digit span, similarities, block design) need speed, working memory or new relations and decline early with ageing and impairment. The explanation concludes that this is why **WAIS** is not the best test of premorbid intelligence.
Hold tests may be sensitive for organic brain damage such as dementia. A deterioration quotient is derived from the difference between 'don't hold' and 'hold' test scores.

**Q45**: block design is the **WAIS** subtest that declines with ageing (non-hold test); hold tests are vocabulary, information, object assembly and picture completion, though the explanation notes the hold-test idea is disputed.
Raven's progressive matrices: a test of **IQ** independent of education and cultural influences; taps general intelligence with visuospatial problem-solving tasks (performance **IQ**).

Raven's progressive matrices = general intellectual ability (multiple-choice tests of abstract reasoning giving culturally unbiased **IQ** estimates) - **NOT** premorbid intelligence (**NART**) and not a frontal, visuospatial or attentional-bias test.
**NART** (National Adult Reading Test): reading is seemingly resistant to organic brain damage, so **NART** taps previous word knowledge and is used to estimate premorbid **IQ**.

To check whether a hospitalised patient's **IQ** has deteriorated, the best test of premorbid **IQ** is the National Adult Reading Test - not Rey-Osterrieth, Luria motor, paired associate learning or Beck's inventory; it is used to estimate premorbid intelligence in English-speaking patients with dementia and other organic brain lesions.

**NART** assesses premorbid intelligence (not visuospatial ability, nonverbal intelligence or frontal function): its validity rests on reading of irregular words being relatively independent of brain damage and a strong predictor of intelligence.
Stroop test: measures set shifting and response inhibition; a test of frontal function and selective attention.

An abnormal Stroop test is keyed to 'attentional bias': the explanation says an abnormal Stroop effect with loss of inhibitory control is seen in frontal lobe lesions, while abnormal modified emotional Stroop interference (e.g. threat words in anxious subjects) is read as mood-congruent attentional bias.

Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (**WCST**): stimulus cards differ in colour, form and number and are sorted by a single principle (e.g. colour, ignoring form and number). Persons with damage to the frontal lobes or the caudate, and some persons with schizophrenia, give abnormal responses.

**WCST** assesses flexibility in problem solving (set shifting in the face of changing reinforcement schedules) - not category fluency, personality traits, visuomotor performance or attention and concentration.

Executive function (planning, initiation, sequencing, coordinating, error detection and correction, set shifting, termination) is tested formally with the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test - not **NART**, Raven's, a vocabulary test or Rey-Osterrieth.

Frontal test deficits: Trail Making Test B, **WCST**, Hayling test (sentence completion), Brixton task, and Trail B of the Halstead-Reitan battery all test set-shifting ability, part of executive functioning.

Alcohol dependence with no memory problems or neurological signs but disorganisation in day-to-day tasks = executive (frontal) decrement, so the trail making test is the impaired performance expected - not orientation, clock drawing, digit span or picture completion.

blocks.title: Neurocognitive deficits in schizophrenia (as listed in the notes)
rows: Deficits in higher order reasoning and perceptual difficulties
Frontal test deficits: far poorer than controls on category test, Wisconsin card sort, paired associates verbal learning test, Trail B of the Halstead-Reitan battery

blocks.text: **Q30**: after severe head injury with grasp reflex, poor judgement, impaired reasoning and impulsivity (frontal signs) the abnormal test is the Wisconsin card sorting test (abnormal in frontal or caudate damage and some schizophrenia).
**Q22**: poor performance on Hayling's test = set-shifting deficit (the explanation says poor performance suggests frontal deficits).

Wechsler Memory Scale-Revised (**WMS-R**): the most widely used memory test battery for adults; yields a memory quotient (**MQ**) corrected for age and generally approximating **WAIS** **IQ**. In amnesic conditions a disproportionately low **MQ** with relatively preserved **IQ** is seen.

Reading a short story with 25 elements and testing immediate and delayed recall (30 minutes) is the Wechsler Memory Scale - one of its verbal subtests - not Rivermead, Rey-Osterrieth, Halstead-Reitan or **WAIS**.

Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test is the one for impairment of everyday memory functioning and for monitoring change after treatment of memory difficulties (task analogues of everyday memory problems; acquired brain injury, dementia, **MS**) - not **WMS**, Halstead-Reitan, Raven's or **TAT**.

Benton Visual Retention Test: a geometric figure is shown for 10 seconds, then the patient draws it from memory (short-term visual memory test). Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test: tests visuomotor coordination, useful for children and adults.

Bender-Gestalt is the instrument keyed for screening cognitive deficits after head injury: it evaluates maturity of the visual-motor system and is also used to assess brain damage and neurological deficits (e.g. as part of a **TBI** battery) - not **NART**, Glasgow Coma Scale, **WAIS** or Raven's.

Halstead-Reitan battery helps determine the location of specific brain lesions: Category test, Tactual performance test, Rhythm test, Finger-oscillation test, Speech-sounds perception test, Trail making test A and B, Critical flicker frequency, Time sense test, Aphasia screening test, Sensory-perceptual tests.

'Wrongly linked' **EMI**-style pairing trap: Rey-Osterrieth is a test of visual memory (recall of learned material), **NOT** of prefrontal pathology - the Wisconsin card sorting test detects prefrontal pathology; Benton = visual memory and paired associates = verbal memory are correct links.

blocks.note: Notes list Hayling (sentence completion) only among set-shifting frontal tests. **Q22**'s explanation adds that two sets of 15 sentences with the last word missing are used, measuring response initiation (part 1) and response suppression (part 2) - not in the notes.

blocks.text: A sentence with the last word missing ('The captain wanted to stay with the sinking ...') = Hayling's test (two sets of 15 sentences; response initiation speed first) - not Brixton, Wisconsin, Stroop or Goldstein.

Hayling is keyed as testing 'verbal fluency and executive function': Part A looks at preprogrammed organising (concentrated attention, verbal initiation, processing speed) and Part B at verbal inhibition and planning.

Poor Brixton performance = a deficit in visuospatial sequencing (rule learning from sequences of stimuli, no verbal response, relatively free from educational and sociocultural bias); often used for executive functioning in stroke, dementia and schizophrenia - contrast with the verbal Hayling.

items.text: **WAIS** test that resists ageing decline = picture completion (hold test).
Digit span tests working memory (immediate) and attention - not semantic or procedural memory, premorbid **IQ** or calculation.
Block design is the **WAIS** subtest that declines with ageing (non-hold test); hold tests include vocabulary and information.
**NART** = reading 50 irregular words to estimate premorbid **IQ**.

bullets.text: WAIS-III 16-89 years; WISC-III under 16; WPPSI-R 4-6.5 years. 11 subtests: 6 verbal + 5 performance, giving verbal, performance and full-scale IQ.

Hold tests (vocabulary, information, object assembly, picture completion) resist ageing; non-hold tests are block design, digit span, similarities, digit symbol; deterioration quotient = difference between them.
NART estimates premorbid IQ; Raven's matrices is independent of education/culture (performance IQ).
Frontal/set-shifting tests: Stroop, WCST, TMT-B, Hayling, Brixton, Trail B of Halstead-Reitan; WCST abnormal in frontal or caudate damage and some schizophrenia.
WMS-R is the commonest adult memory battery; in amnesia MQ is disproportionately low with IQ relatively preserved.
Benton Visual Retention = short-term visual memory (figure for 10 s); Bender = visuomotor coordination; Halstead-Reitan localises lesions.
WAIS hold tests (vocabulary, information, object assembly, picture completion) resist brain damage and ageing.
Raven's = general intellectual ability; NART = premorbid IQ; WCST = set shifting.

blocks.text: Consciousness is a state characterised by awareness of self and environment and an ability to respond to environmental factors; it has two components - arousal (wakefulness) and awareness (attentional processing).

Arousal depends on an intact ascending reticular activating system (**ARAS**). Thalamocortical connections generate rhythmical bursts of neuronal activity (20-40 Hz) that are in desynchrony by default; the **ARAS**, acting via the thalamic intralaminar nuclei, synchronises these oscillations, and arousal is directly proportional to the degree of synchrony achieved. Absence of arousal produces stupor and coma.

Maintenance of attention appears to require an intact right frontal lobe. Small lesions of the **ARAS** are enough to produce a stuporous state, but large bilateral lesions are needed at cortical level to cause the same depression in alertness.

blocks.title: States related to coma
rows: Appears asleep but when vigorously stimulated may become alert (eye opening, ocular movement); most patients have diffuse organic cerebral dysfunction. Caloric testing: organic stupor shows tonic deviation; psychiatric stupor (catatonia/depression) shows ocular nystagmus

Immobility and eye closure with little or no vocalisation; sleep/wake cycles seen (eye opening); little movement to painful stimuli; hallmark = absence of spasticity and rigidity. **CJD** can present with akinetic mutism before death
Diencephalic or bilateral anterior cingulate damage; lesions interfering with reticular/cortical integration but sparing corticospinal pathways

Isolated action of **ARAS** and thalamus without higher cortical influence; fully established state almost invariably shows spasticity and rigidity of limbs (absent in akinetic mutism); early on the two are indistinguishable

Total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei; can open eyes and elevate/depress eyes to command; horizontal eye movements usually lost; patient opens eyes voluntarily (not spontaneously as in vegetative state)
Infarction of ventral pons, pontine tumours, pontine haemorrhage, central pontine myelinolysis, head injury, brain stem encephalitis

blocks.text: There is some debate about whether akinetic mutism should be clearly differentiated from the vegetative state.

**Q37**: caloric testing differentiates organic from psychiatric stuporous states - tonic deviation in organic stupor, nystagmus in psychiatric stupor (the fast phase reflects correction after tonic deviation and needs the patient to be conscious).

blocks.note: Notes describe the vegetative state as isolated **ARAS**/thalamic function with spasticity and rigidity. **Q7**'s explanation (Monti et al.) lists the defining features as cycles of eye opening and closing (sleep-wake appearance), complete lack of awareness of self/environment, and complete or partial preservation of hypothalamic and brainstem autonomic functions - not in the notes.

bullets.text: Consciousness = arousal (wakefulness) + awareness (attentional processing).
Arousal needs an intact ARAS; ARAS via thalamic intralaminar nuclei synchronises 20-40 Hz thalamocortical oscillations; no arousal gives stupor and coma.
Attention needs an intact right frontal lobe; small ARAS lesions cause stupor but cortical lesions must be large and bilateral.
Caloric testing: organic stupor = tonic deviation; psychiatric stupor (catatonia/depression) = nystagmus.
Akinetic mutism (diencephalic/bilateral anterior cingulate) lacks spasticity/rigidity; established vegetative state almost invariably shows them.
Locked-in syndrome: ventral pontine lesion, total paralysis below the 3rd nerve nuclei, eye elevation/depression and voluntary eye opening preserved.

blocks.text: Attention can be tested clinically using serial 7s, digit span, spelling 'world' backwards, or reciting the months of the year or days of the week in reverse.

Serial 7s is commonly used but is frequently performed incorrectly by the elderly and by patients with impaired attention. Reverse-order months of the year is a highly over-learned sequence and a preferred measure of sustained attention.

Digit span is a relatively pure test of attention that depends on working memory. It is impaired in delirium, focal left frontal damage, aphasia and moderate to severe dementia, but preserved in the amnesic syndrome (e.g. Korsakoff's syndrome or medial temporal lobe damage). Normal digit span is 7+/-2, varying with age and general intellectual ability; in the elderly or intellectually impaired, 5 can be normal. Reverse digit span is usually one less than forward span.

blocks.title: Orientation
rows: Usually assessed in time, place and person; intact orientation does not exclude a memory disorder

Most helpful test; should include the time of day. Many healthy people do not know the exact date; inaccuracy of two days or less is normal. Time intervals (e.g. length of time spent in hospital) are poorly monitored in delirium, moderate to severe dementia and the amnesic syndrome
Name, age, date of birth; disorientation to one's own name is usually seen only in psychogenic amnesia
Affected in reduplicative paramnesia, seen in delirium

blocks.text: **Q19**: orientation to time is the first domain affected in delirium (time orientation is the most helpful and is affected early; orientation is not a particularly sensitive cognitive test and intact orientation does not exclude a memory disorder).
**Q36**: spelling the word '**WORLD**' backwards tests attention (alongside serial 7s, digit span and reciting months in reverse).
Immediate repetition of 3 items in the **MMSE** tests registration; recall is tested by asking for the items again after a distraction (delayed recall) - not recognition, digit span or fluency.
Digit span is a test of working memory (immediate) and attention - not semantic memory, procedural memory, premorbid **IQ** or calculation ability.

bullets.text: Attention tests: serial 7s, digit span, 'world' backwards, months/days in reverse; reverse months is preferred for sustained attention.
Serial 7s is often done wrongly by the elderly and by patients with impaired attention.
Digit span (attention, working memory) is impaired in delirium, left frontal damage, aphasia, moderate-severe dementia; preserved in amnesic syndrome.
Normal digit span 7+/-2 (5 can be normal in elderly/intellectually impaired); reverse span usually one less.
Orientation: time is most helpful (error of two days or less normal); intact orientation does not exclude a memory disorder.
Disorientation to own name is usually psychogenic amnesia; place orientation is affected in reduplicative paramnesia (delirium).

blocks.text: Executive function includes planning, initiation, sequencing, coordinating, error detection, error correction, set shifting and termination, and is closely allied to judgement, problem solving, impulse control and abstract reasoning. It is generally believed to be a dorsolateral frontal lobe function and depends on intact frontal-subcortical circuits.

blocks.mnemonic: PISCEEST = Plan, Initiate, Sequence, Coordinate, Err-detect, Err-correct, Set-shift, Terminate

blocks.text: Impulsivity reflects failure of response inhibition and is seen in inferior frontal pathology; it can be assessed with the Go-No-Go task (tap once for a single tap, withhold for two taps). It can be made harder by changing the rule after several trials (e.g. 'tap once when I tap twice, and not at all when I tap once').

Task switching and inhibition of perseverative responses can be assessed by asking the patient to copy a short sequence of alternating squares and triangles and continue across the page; perseveration in drawing one shape may be seen in frontal deficits, but the test is relatively insensitive.
The cognitive estimates test (e.g. height of the Post Office Tower, population of London, speed of a typical racehorse) may prompt bizarre or improbable responses in frontal/executive dysfunction.

Similarity questions assess inferential reasoning: simple pairs ('apples and oranges', 'desk and chair') first, then abstract pairs ('love and hate', 'sculpture and symphony'). Patients typically answer concretely that the objects are 'different' or 'not similar'. Proverb testing probably measures a similar skill but is highly dependent on educational and cultural background.
**Q30**: grasp reflex, poor judgement, impaired reasoning and impulsivity after head injury point to a frontal lobe lesion, for which the Wisconsin card sorting test is the abnormal test.

blocks.subtopic: Negative symptoms of schizophrenia and the DLPFC
blocks.note: Not in these notes. The negative symptoms are keyed to hypoactivation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex: the explanation says positive symptoms may relate to excessive subcortical **DA** transmission and negative symptoms to a concomitant deficit in cortical **DA** transmission, with fMRI showing reduced prefrontal activation (**VLPFC**, **DLPFC**, anterior cingulate) in unmedicated patients.

Not in these notes. The keyed neuropsychological theory is orbitofrontal striatal executive dysfunction: the explanation describes **ADHD** as impaired behavioural inhibition leading to executive function deficits, with dysfunction of reward circuitry including orbitofrontal systems.

bullets.text: Executive function: planning, initiation, sequencing, coordination, error detection/correction, set shifting, termination - dorsolateral frontal, frontal-subcortical circuits.
Impulsivity = failure of response inhibition (inferior frontal); test with Go-No-Go.
Alternating squares/triangles copying shows perseveration but is relatively insensitive.
Cognitive estimates test gives bizarre/improbable answers in frontal dysfunction.
Similarities: concrete answers ('different', 'not similar') show impaired abstraction; proverbs depend on education and culture.

blocks.title: Visual processing streams
rows: Spatial position and orientation in the parietal lobe
Store of semantic knowledge in the temporal lobes

blocks.text: Information from the visual cortex is directed to the temporal or parietal cortex via one of the two streams. The frontal eye fields are important in directing attention towards targets in the visual field. Neglect and constructional apraxia are disorders of visuospatial function.

Neglect of personal and extrapersonal space is usually due to right hemisphere lesions, usually inferior parietal or prefrontal. The left side of personal and extrapersonal space is represented only in the right parietal lobe, whereas the right side gets bilateral representation; hence a left-sided lesion rarely results in neglect but a right-sided lesion can cause left-sided neglect.

Neglect can be uncovered by simultaneous bilateral sensory or visual stimulation or by line bisection of variable length lines; letter and star cancellation tasks are similar formal tasks. Visual neglect may produce failure to groom half the body or to eat food on one side of a plate; in extreme cases patients may have anosognosia and deny they are hemiplegic or that the limb belongs to them.

Dressing and constructional apraxia are termed apraxias but are best considered visuospatial rather than motor impairments. Copying 3-D shapes (wire cube), interlocking pentagons (as in **MMSE**) or constructing a clock-face are good tests of constructional ability and may also show neglect; dressing apraxia is tested by having the patient put on clothing turned inside out.

**Q21**: inability to copy intersecting polygons on the **MMSE** suggests visuospatial deficits (inability to draw shapes or construct geometrical patterns; mostly the nondominant hemisphere is damaged).
**Q1**: a man who leaves food on one side of his plate and bisects a line near the right end has a right parietal lesion (neglect from right hemisphere lesions).

bullets.text: Dorsal ('where') stream = spatial position/orientation in parietal lobe; ventral ('what') stream = semantic knowledge in temporal lobes.
Frontal eye fields direct attention to visual targets; neglect and constructional apraxia are visuospatial disorders.
Neglect usually from right hemisphere lesions (inferior parietal or prefrontal): left space is represented only on the right, right space bilaterally.
Neglect uncovered by bilateral simultaneous stimulation, line bisection, letter/star cancellation; may cause failure to groom or eat one side, and anosognosia.
Dressing and constructional apraxias are visuospatial, not motor; test with wire cube, MMSE interlocking pentagons, clock face, inside-out clothing.

blocks.title: Classification of memory
rows: Seconds; closely related to working memory
Meanings; memory for word meaning and general knowledge
Events; time-locked memory for personal events ('when and where'), includes anterograde and retrograde memory; depends on the hippocampal-diencephalic system
Skills and procedures, e.g. car driving

blocks.text: Working memory is the very limited-capacity system that retains information for a few seconds. It comprises a central executive system (attentional system, dorsolateral prefrontal) and at least two buffer systems - the visuospatial sketchpad (right hemisphere) and the phonological loop (left hemisphere).
The term 'short term' memory is applied, confusingly, to a number of different memory problems and has no convincing anatomical or psychological correlate.

blocks.title: Brain structures involved in memory
rows: Left hippocampus encodes declarative verbal and right hippocampus non-verbal memories; also serves navigational memory and memory of object location (hippocampal place code in animal studies). Unilateral lesions are compensated well - clinically significant amnesia does not occur

Rates the emotional importance of experience and regulates hippocampal activity accordingly; emotional memory and emotional face processing; memory consolidation depends on emotional input. Damage leads to loss of fear conditioning (and loss of maternal behaviour in monkeys); learning and consolidation can still occur without emotional valence and arousal
Diencephalon (dorsal medial nucleus of thalamus, mamillary bodies)
Associated with new learning; damage leads to diencephalic amnesia seen in Korsakoff syndrome
Cerebellum, striatum, amygdala, parts of neocortex (including motor area)
Thought (though speculative) to be involved in non-declarative procedural memory storage

blocks.text: In most cases of memory loss procedural memory is intact. A deficit in procedural memory with preserved declarative memory may be seen in Parkinson's disease, in which dopaminergic neurons of the nigrostriatal tract degenerate.

Long-term potentiation (**LTP**): strengthening of the connection between two neurons on repeated communication; may be the neuronal basis of memory. It is mediated by **NMDA**-mediated Ca2+ entry in glutamate neurons. Learning increases branching and synapse formation and may influence neurogenesis.

**Q20**: the amnesia of Korsakoff's syndrome is episodic - anterograde and retrograde amnesia with episodic memory impairment, confabulation, lack of insight and apathy; the retrograde amnesia extends back at least 25 to 30 years (not implicit/procedural).

Anterograde amnesia with preserved insight is keyed to hippocampal amnesia (not psychogenic amnesia, orbitofrontal lesions or Pick's disease); the explanation says anterograde amnesia is seen most frequently after injury to the medial temporal lobes (amygdala, hippocampal formation) or the diencephalon.

Amnesia is a term used either for pure memory deficits (mostly episodic) or cognitive deficits where memory loss is predominant and not congruent with the level of loss in other domains. Generally both anterograde and retrograde memory loss occur in parallel, such as in Alzheimer's disease or head injury.

blocks.title: Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia
rows: Forgetting newly encountered information from the time of a lesion
Loss of memory of past events that happened before the lesion was sustained
Forgetfulness regarding appointments, losing items around the home, inability to remember a conversation leading to repeated questions
Loss of memory of past events such as jobs, holidays; not able to remember the topography of a route and getting lost
Relatively pure anterograde amnesia may be seen with hippocampal damage, e.g. herpes simplex encephalitis, focal temporal lobe tumours, infarction

blocks.text: Being unable to recall any events of a head-injury admission even two years later, with no other memory problem, is anterograde amnesia - no memory trace was formed for that period; it is not retrograde amnesia, confabulation, episodic memory loss or dissociative loss.
Confabulation (e.g. in Korsakoff's syndrome) might be grandiose or delusional, but more often involves the misordering and fusion of real memories that end up being retrieved out of context.

A transient amnesic syndrome with pronounced anterograde and variable retrograde amnesia is seen in transient global amnesia (**TGA**), while 'memory lacunes' and repeated brief episodes of memory loss suggest transient epileptic amnesia (**TEA**).

Transient global amnesia: complete, reversible anterograde and retrograde memory loss lasting up to 24 hours, patient bewildered but alert and repeatedly asking questions, persistent loss of memory for the attack - not **CJD**, Alzheimer's, **NPH** or Parkinson's.

Ribot's law of retrograde amnesia: 'The dissolution of memory is inversely related to the recency of the event'. Recent memories are more likely to be lost than remote ones in organic amnesia (not always the case).

**Q26**: Ribot's law = the gradient of episodic memory loss runs from the most recent to more remote events (recent memories lost before remote ones in organic amnesia, with some exceptions) - the reverse of the distractor 'remote memories lost before recent ones'.

Ribot's law = temporally graded retrograde amnesia: newly formed memories (just before the brain injury) are lost more than older ones - not interference theory, decay theory, law of effect or Yerkes-Dodson.
**Q42**: when the temporal order of memory is disturbed leading to out-of-context retrieval, the term is confabulation (seen in Korsakoff's syndrome and also in dementias).

Semantic dementia: a variant of frontotemporal dementia. Patients complain of loss of words; vocabulary diminishes and substitute words such as 'thing' are used, with parallel impairment in appreciating the meaning of individual words, first involving infrequent or unusual words.

Semantic memory (word meaning and general knowledge; anterior temporal lobe) is checked at the bedside with object naming and defining word meanings - not copying pentagons, category fluency with digit-symbol, serial subtraction or letter fluency; semantic breakdown shows loss of words, diminished vocabulary and stock words such as 'thing'.

Word-finding difficulty is common in anxiety and ageing but is variable and not associated with impaired comprehension - in stark contrast to the anomia of semantic dementia, which is relentlessly progressive and associated with atrophy of the anterior temporal lobe, usually on the left.

**Q39**: better preserved letter fluency but poor category fluency = semantic dementia (category fluency taps semantic memory, whose key substrate is the anterior temporal lobe; this domain is affected earlier than phonological/letter fluency in semantic dementia).

Working memory deficits present as lapses in concentration and attention (losing one's train of thought, inability to process a complex task as components are not retained long enough). Basal ganglia and white matter diseases may present with predominantly working memory deficits.

Dissociative amnesia is not an organic syndrome: loss of memory of important recent events that is partial, patchy and selective; can occur as part of dissociative fugue. It is episodic memory loss (retrograde only, no anterograde deficit) for events from a discrete period (minutes to years). The problem is not inefficient retrieval but strikingly complete unavailability of memories formed normally and previously accessible; the forgotten events are generally traumatic or stressful.

**Q6**: wandering after the sudden death of a husband = fugue state, a form of dissociative amnesia (unplanned travel or wandering, sometimes with a new identity; profound but reversible amnesia for personal identity after trauma or stress; usually short-lived).

blocks.note: **Q40**, **Q44** and **Q47** test dementia presentations not covered in the memory notes: vascular dementia with retained insight and patchy cognitive impairment (**Q40**); early Alzheimer's with name-forgetting but preserved day-to-day function (**Q44**); frontotemporal dementia with relative preservation of day-to-day episodic memory and semantic dementia in the temporal variant (**Q47**; the notes cover semantic dementia only as a frontotemporal variant with word loss).

blocks.text: Vascular dementia = patchy/uneven cognitive impairment with insight, judgement and personality relatively well preserved - so a patient who retains full insight into progressive cognitive decline is keyed to vascular dementia over frontotemporal dementia, **CJD** or Huntington's.

Early Alzheimer's disease = forgetting trivial details, names and faces while day-to-day functional abilities stay largely preserved - the keyed answer over **CJD**, Pick's, vascular dementia and Binswanger's.

bullets.text: Memory by duration: immediate (seconds), recent (minutes-days), remote (months-years); by encoding: explicit (semantic = meanings, episodic = events) and implicit (procedural).
Working memory = central executive (dorsolateral prefrontal) + visuospatial sketchpad (right) + phonological loop (left).

Left hippocampus encodes verbal, right non-verbal memory; unilateral hippocampal lesions compensated; amygdala = emotional memory/fear conditioning; thalamic dorsal medial nucleus and mamillary bodies = diencephalic (Korsakoff) amnesia.
Procedural memory usually intact in amnesia; lost with preserved declarative memory in Parkinson's; anterior temporal lobe is key for semantic memory.
LTP (NMDA-mediated Ca2+ entry in glutamate neurons) may be the neuronal basis of memory.
Anterograde = new information after lesion (hippocampal damage e.g. HSV encephalitis); retrograde = events before lesion; confabulation = misordered fusion of real memories.
TGA = pronounced anterograde with variable retrograde amnesia; Ribot's law = recent memories lost before remote ones.

Dissociative amnesia: retrograde only, patchy/selective, memories formed normally but unavailable, usually traumatic; semantic dementia: progressive loss of word meaning with left anterior temporal atrophy.
Vascular dementia: patchy impairment, insight preserved; early Alzheimer's: names forgotten, function preserved.

blocks.text: Aphasia is a higher-level language defect despite intact hearing, sound production and articulation mechanisms. It is almost always organic, and naming defects (anomia) accompany any aphasia in varying degrees.

Sound received by the ears is transmitted to Wernicke's area and the auditory association cortex, which processes the language component. The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke's area to Broca's area (different from the uncinate fasciculus, which interconnects the anterior temporal and inferior frontal gyrus). Broca's area is the higher motor area of language production; its signals are relayed to the motor area to coordinate delivery via tongue, lips and vocal cords.

blocks.title: Three components of language
rows: Intact Broca's area and its forward connections
Intact Wernicke's area and its connection with association cortex and sensory input
No high-level processing; occurs if Broca's, Wernicke's and the arcuate fasciculus are intact (does not need relay from either area to higher association areas)

blocks.title: Types of aphasia (adapted from Harrison's Textbook of Internal Medicine, 15th ed.)

blocks.text: **Q9**: loss of fluency and repetition with preserved comprehension = Broca's aphasia (not transcortical motor, which keeps repetition, nor conduction aphasia).

blocks.title: Broca's vs Wernicke's aphasia
rows: Non-fluent, laboured with interruptions and pauses; telegraphic
Fluent but highly paraphasic, with strings of neologisms and circumlocutions ('jargon aphasia')
Function words (prepositions, conjunctions) most affected; a good degree of meaning-appropriate nouns and verbs still produced
Many function words but few substantive nouns or verbs referring to specific actions
Abnormal word order and characteristic agrammatism
Voluminous but uninformative output, at times mimicking schizophrenic speech disturbance
Not stated in this passage (see aphasia table: intact)
Impaired for both spoken and written language

blocks.text: Broca's aphasia is 'non-fluent aphasia' (also non-fluent expressive dysphasia): fluency and repetition are affected while comprehension is preserved - not fluent, conduction, nominal or jargon aphasia.

In a Broca's area lesion, comprehension is the preserved feature (the 'which is seen' option); speech is slow, halting and rarely grammatical, with inflections (-ed) and function words (the, and) dropped - naming, inflection, repetition and fluency are not preserved.

Nominal (anomic) aphasia is keyed to the parietal lobe: the explanation says that although many believed damage to Broca's or Wernicke's area was the main cause of anomia, current studies show damage in the left parietal lobe is the epicentre.

**Q16**: a stroke patient calling apples 'oranges' shows semantic paraphasia (mis-selection of words through semantic confusion, e.g. 'bread' for 'food'); phonemic paraphasia is sound-based (e.g. 'shark' for 'sharp').

blocks.note: Notes describe Wernicke's aphasia as 'highly paraphasic' but never define semantic or phonemic paraphasia; **Q16**'s explanation supplies both definitions.

blocks.title: Pure language syndromes
rows: Speaks, reads and writes fluently; comprehension impaired only for spoken language
Bilateral (or left-sided with disrupted connections to non-dominant circuit) damage to the superior temporal pole is suspected
Speaks normally, comprehends speech, writes spontaneously and to dictation; reading comprehension impaired
Almost always infarct of left posterior cerebral artery affecting splenium of corpus callosum and left visual cortex; the intact right visual cortex sees but cannot do lexical word processing
Spoken language cannot be produced clearly, but comprehends, reads and writes
Isolated inability to write while other language faculties are preserved

blocks.text: Pure word deafness spares reading and writing: the patient speaks, reads and writes fluently, with comprehension impaired only for spoken language (bilateral superior temporal pole damage suspected) - in Wernicke's aphasia comprehension is impaired for both spoken and written language.

Speaks, comprehends, writes spontaneously and to dictation but cannot comprehend reading = pure word blindness (alexia without agraphia), not pure word deafness, jargon, Broca's or Wernicke's aphasia.

Alexia **WITH** agraphia: right visual field defect is the expected feature (right homonymous hemianopia is commonly associated; colour recognition and auditory comprehension often intact); alexia without agraphia occurs in occipitotemporal lesions, whereas alexia with agraphia often results from a left angular gyral lesion.

items.text: Alexia without agraphia most commonly involves the corpus callosum (splenium) with a left posterior cerebral artery infarct; the person sees with the right visual cortex but cannot read, yet writes normally.
Alexia without agraphia (pure alexia) is seen in posterior cerebral territory lesions - not middle meningeal, anterior or middle cerebral territory or **PICA**.

Non-fluent aphasia is associated with lesions in or near Broca's area (not insula, parietal operculum, anterior cingulate or superior temporal gyrus); temporal and parietal lobes are usually not impaired.
Non-fluent expressive dysphasia is commonly seen in frontotemporal dementia (Pick's disease) - not Lewy body dementia, **PSP**, Parkinson's or **CJD**.
Sudden right arm weakness with inability to understand speech = (receptive) aphasia from Wernicke's area damage - not aphemia, alexia or agraphia.
Deaf patients' language cortex is organised like that of hearing people: left temporal lesions cause comprehension deficits in sign language users, and Broca's area serves production.

bullets.text: Aphasia = higher-level language defect with intact hearing/articulation; almost always organic; anomia accompanies any aphasia.
Wernicke's area (comprehension) - arcuate fasciculus - Broca's area (fluency); repetition needs all three intact.
Broca's: fluency lost, repetition lost, comprehension intact; Wernicke's: fluency intact, repetition and comprehension lost; conduction: only repetition lost (fluency and comprehension intact).
Transcortical sensory: only comprehension lost (with naming); transcortical motor: only fluency lost (with naming).
Broca's: telegraphic, agrammatic, function words most affected; Wernicke's: fluent jargon with neologisms, impaired comprehension, little substantive content.
Pure word blindness (alexia without agraphia): left PCA infarct, splenium of corpus callosum and left visual cortex; writing preserved.
Pure word deafness: only spoken comprehension impaired; pure agraphia: isolated writing loss; pure word dumbness: cannot produce speech but comprehends, reads, writes.
Broca's: fluency/repetition lost, comprehension preserved; pure word deafness spares reading and writing.

facts.label: Broca's aphasia
facts.value: Fluency lost, repetition lost, comprehension intact

facts.label: Conduction aphasia
facts.value: Repetition lost; fluency and comprehension intact

facts.label: Transcortical motor aphasia
facts.value: Fluency lost; repetition and comprehension intact

blocks.text: Damasio and Geschwind (1985) defined apraxia as varying combinations of the following disturbances, in order of progressive dysfunction: failure to produce the correct movement to verbal command; failure to imitate a movement performed by the examiner; failure to perform a movement correctly in response to a seen object; failure to handle an object correctly.

Labels such as limb kinetic, ideomotor and ideational are seldom useful clinically; it is more helpful to describe apraxia by region (orobuccal or limb) and to describe impaired performance, recording both spatial and sequencing errors on several types of task.
Apraxia has limited localising ability, but the left parietal and frontal lobes appear most important. Progressive, isolated limb apraxia is virtually diagnostic of corticobasal degeneration.

blocks.title: Functional classification of apraxia
rows: Inability to construct elements into a meaningful whole, e.g. inability to draw or copy simple diagrams or figures
Right cerebral hemisphere, often parietal lobe
Impairment in carrying out sequences of actions (multiple-step task) using various objects in the correct order; the patient does not know 'what' to do
Ideomotor (most common type among all apraxias)

Disorder of goal-directed movement: the patient knows what to do but not how; impaired pantomiming of tool use, with body-part-as-object substitution (finger used as toothbrush) and abnormal orientation of the body part; improves on imitation and with the actual tool; tool use more affected than gestures
Mainly left hemisphere; frontal and parietal association areas. Unilateral left hemisphere lesions in right-handers produce bilateral deficits, usually less severe in the left than the right limb

blocks.text: Unable to mimic hammering a nail on request = ideomotor apraxia (disorder of goal-directed movement: the patient knows what to do but not how; tool use more affected than spontaneous gestures; pantomime impaired) - not constructional or dressing apraxia, finger agnosia or visual object agnosia.

blocks.title: Regional classification of apraxia
rows: Inability to coordinate and carry out facial and lip movements such as whistling, winking, coughing on command
Most frequent type of all focal-lesion-related apraxia syndromes; left inferior frontal lobe and insula; commonly accompanies the aphasia caused by lesions of Broca's area
Loss of hand and finger dexterity from inability to connect or isolate individual movements; affects tool use and gestures, especially distal finger movements; can be ideomotor or ideational type
Dominant frontoparietal or primary motor cortex
Apraxia of speech, apraxia of eyelid opening and apraxia of gait

bullets.text: Apraxia: failure of movement to command, imitation, seen object, or object handling, in order of progressive dysfunction (Damasio and Geschwind).
Describe apraxia by region (orobuccal/limb) rather than by ideomotor/ideational labels; left parietal and frontal lobes most important.
Progressive isolated limb apraxia is virtually diagnostic of corticobasal degeneration.
Constructional = right hemisphere (parietal); ideational = left parieto-occipital/parietotemporal, does not know what to do; ideomotor = most common, left frontal/parietal, knows what but not how.
Buccofacial apraxia: most frequent, left inferior frontal/insula, accompanies Broca's aphasia; limb-kinetic: loss of distal finger dexterity, dominant frontoparietal/primary motor cortex.
Other variants: apraxia of speech, eyelid opening, gait.
Cannot mimic hammering a nail = ideomotor apraxia.

blocks.title: Visual object agnosia: apperceptive vs associative
rows: Normal vision but cannot identify and name objects
Preserved - can name objects from description or touch
Anterior left temporal lobe lesions often seen

blocks.text: Visual object agnosia is failure of object recognition despite adequate perception. To test, assess visual object naming/description, tactile naming, naming described objects, and giving semantic information about unnamed items.

Prosopagnosia: the ability to recognise familiar faces is affected, but clues such as voice and gait can aid identification. The deficit is often not restricted to faces - fine-grained identification within categories (types of fruits and flowers) may be impaired. Underlying semantic knowledge of a person is not disrupted, so the patient can usually describe the facial features of a named person.

Face processing is a bilateral function, with more key areas possibly on the right. Acquired prosopagnosia is usually associated with bilateral or right-sided lesions of the occipital-temporal junction (fusiform gyrus). Rare prosopagnosia after left-sided lesions in left-handed subjects is attributed to reversed hemispheric specialisation for face processing.

**Q4**: loss of recognising her husband's face but recognising him by voice and routines = bilateral occipito-temporal lesion (acquired prosopagnosia: bilateral or right-sided occipital-temporal junction/fusiform gyrus lesions).

blocks.title: Colour deficits
rows: Loss of ability to discriminate colours (often associated with pure alexia)
Loss of ability to retrieve colour information stored in the semantic knowledge base (e.g. 'What colour is a banana?')
Disorder of colour naming despite intact perception and colour knowledge ('What colour is this?')
Medial occipitotemporal damage due to left posterior cerebral artery infarction
Disconnection of the language structures in the temporal lobe from the visual cortex

bullets.text: Visual object agnosia = failed object recognition despite adequate perception.
Apperceptive: normal vision, cannot name objects but semantic knowledge preserved (names from description/touch); bilateral occipitotemporal infarction.
Associative: stored semantic knowledge affected; anterior left temporal lesions.
Prosopagnosia: cannot recognise faces (voice/gait help); semantic knowledge of the person intact; may extend to fine within-category identification.
Acquired prosopagnosia: bilateral or right occipital-temporal junction (fusiform gyrus) lesions.
Colour: achromatopsia (cannot discriminate; left PCA infarct), colour agnosia (cannot retrieve colour knowledge), colour anomia (naming disorder; disconnection).

blocks.text: Acalculia is the inability to read, write and comprehend numbers; it is **NOT** the same as anarithmetrica, the inability to perform arithmetical calculations. It can be tested by simple calculation, writing numbers to dictation, copying and reading numbers aloud, and giving reasons for calculated answers.

Balint's syndrome results from bilateral superior parieto-occipital damage (disruption of the dorsal 'where' stream linking visual and parietal association areas). Possible causes include carbon monoxide poisoning, infarction and Alzheimer's disease.

blocks.title: Balint's syndrome triad
rows: Inability to attend to more than one item of a complex scene at a time
Inability to guide reaching or pointing despite adequate vision
Inability to voluntarily direct saccades to a visual target

blocks.text: **Q25**: simultanagnosia is associated with Balint's syndrome (not Anton's, Gerstmann or Marchiafava-Bignami); the explanation adds that fields may be full to gross stimuli and oculocephalic reflexes are intact.

Gerstmann syndrome: four primary symptoms - dysgraphia/agraphia, dyscalculia/acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation. The full tetrad is rare but occurs with lesions in the dominant angular and supramarginal gyri (parietal lobe).
Anton's syndrome occurs in bilateral occipital damage: the patient denies any deficit and may even attempt to walk and navigate without success.

Marchiafava-Bignami disease: symmetrical demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum and adjacent anterior commissure, mostly seen in alcoholics using red wine excessively (not clear whether impurities are implicated). Presents with sudden stupor or coma and seizures; a chronic onset of dementia and/or gait problems with spasticity is also reported.

blocks.note: **Q25**'s explanation lists additional causes of Balint's syndrome: watershed infarction, leucodystrophy and the posterior cortical variant of Alzheimer's disease; the notes list only carbon monoxide poisoning, infarction and Alzheimer's disease.

bullets.text: Acalculia (cannot read, write, comprehend numbers) is not anarithmetrica (cannot perform arithmetic).
Balint's: bilateral superior parieto-occipital damage, dorsal 'where' stream disrupted; triad = simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia.
Balint's causes: carbon monoxide poisoning, infarction, Alzheimer's disease.
Gerstmann's tetrad: dysgraphia, dyscalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation - dominant angular and supramarginal gyri.
Anton's: bilateral occipital damage with denial of blindness/deficit.
Marchiafava-Bignami: corpus callosum and anterior commissure demyelination/necrosis in red-wine alcoholics; stupor/coma, seizures, chronic dementia/gait problems with spasticity.

blocks.text: Olfactory nerve (**CN** I) is the only sensory nerve with no thalamic relay. Unilateral anosmia should raise suspicion of a lesion affecting the olfactory nerve filaments, bulb, tract or stria. Because cortical representation of smell in the piriform cortex is bilateral, a unilateral lesion distal to the decussation (temporal/uncinate) causes no olfactory impairment.

Frontal meningiomas can cause unilateral anosmia; head injury is probably the most common cause of disruption of the olfactory fibres. Hyposmia is an early feature of Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's dementia and may precede motor and cognitive signs respectively; impaired sense of smell is seen in some patients at ==50%== risk of Parkinsonism.

blocks.title: Optic nerve (CN II) syndromes and lesions
rows: Lesion anterior to optic chiasm, e.g. optic nerve itself or retina
Optic chiasmatic lesion, e.g. craniopharyngioma, pineal tumours
Lesions of the right-sided optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiations and striate cortex (any retrochiasmatic structure)
Lesions of the left retrochiasmatic structures
Optic irradiation lesion at the temporal lobes of the contralateral side
Optic irradiation lesion at the parietal lobes of the contralateral side

blocks.text: Upper quadrantanopia from a unilateral cortical lesion = the lower bank of the calcarine fissure (primary visual cortex; its lower-bank neurons carry the upper visual fields via the lateral geniculate nucleus) - not frontal, parietal-operculum, inferior parietal or medial temporal sites.

Bitemporal hemianopia is keyed to a pituitary tumour: the explanation says most adults present with visual failure and optic atrophy and bitemporal hemianopia is found in about one-third at diagnosis, though usually asymmetrical and unpredictable in evolution.
**Q35**: bitemporal hemianopia = optic chiasma lesion (e.g. pineal tumours, craniopharyngioma).

Hemianopia is a field defect covering roughly half the field; vertical hemianopia can be nasal or temporal, horizontal/altitudinal hemianopia superior or inferior; one-fourth of the field affected is quadrantanopia. Bilateral field defects are homonymous when they affect the identical portion of vision in both fields.

blocks.title: Funnel vision vs tunnel vision
rows: In organic visual system defect the field projected at 2 m is larger than at 1 m
Absence of disparity between 2 m and 1 m fields
Glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa, post-papilloedema optic atrophy, bilateral occipital infarcts with macular sparing
Hysteria or malingering (patchy spirals of field loss)

blocks.text: **Q18**: in suspected conversion disorder with sudden blindness and normal investigations, tunnel vision on perimetry supports the diagnosis (absence of projected disparity between near and far fields; patchy spirals of field loss seen in hysteria and malingering).

Cortical blindness often results from simultaneous bilateral posterior cerebral artery occlusion. Patients often have bilateral homonymous hemianopia with a small central field around fixation (macular sparing or keyhole vision) or complete blindness; occasionally they deny the defect (Anton's syndrome).

Pupillary light reflex: afferent fibres in each optic nerve (some crossing at the chiasm) pass to both lateral geniculate bodies and relay to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei (midbrain) via the pretectal nucleus; efferent parasympathetic fibres pass via the third nerve to the ciliary ganglion and the pupil. Light constricts the illuminated pupil (direct reflex) and the contralateral pupil (consensual reflex).

Convergence/accommodation reflex: fixation on a near object requires convergence with pupillary constriction. Afferent fibres in each optic nerve, via both lateral geniculate bodies, relay to the convergence centre, which receives muscle spindle afferents from the extraocular muscles (principally medial recti, third nerve); the efferent route is convergence centre to Edinger-Westphal nucleus, ciliary ganglion and pupils.

Pupils that accommodate but do not react show light-near dissociation. Two important types: Argyll Robertson pupil (neurosyphilis and diabetes; more common these days) and Adie pupil (peripheral pupillary defect producing a tonic pupil). **ARP** is due to an afferent defect in the pupillary reflex pathway, possibly pretectal.

blocks.mnemonic: ARP = Accommodation Reflex Present (light reflex absent)

blocks.text: **Q43**: accommodation reflexes present with small, irregular pupils that do not react to light = Argyll Robertson pupils (syphilitic or diabetic neural damage; frequently quite miotic and irregular; recalcitrant to pharmacological dilation).

Small irregular pupils with absent light reflexes but present accommodation = Argyll Robertson pupils (not Marcus Gunn or senile pupil); the explanation says they came to be considered pathognomonic of tabes dorsalis, general paresis and neurovascular syphilis.

blocks.title: Cranial nerves III-VI
rows: Nucleus in midbrain; supplies levator palpebrae superioris, superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique

Paralysis of ipsilateral upper eyelid and pupil, unable to adduct or look up/down, eye frequently turned out (exotropia). Nuclear lesion causes bilateral ptosis. Only ocular motor nerve lesion causing diplopia in more than one direction. Pupil-sparing paralysis occurs in diabetes mellitus, vasculitides and certain brainstem lesions (e.g. multiple sclerosis)
Nucleus in midbrain; innervates superior oblique
Allows a person to view the tip of the nose

Nucleus from midbrain (mesencephalic) through pons (main sensory and motor) to cervical region (spinal tract); sensory to face and muscles of mastication; divisions **V1** ophthalmic, **V2** maxillary, **V3** mandibular

blocks.text: Romberg test evaluates vestibular control of balance: standing with feet together and eyes closed, the patient tends to fall toward the side of vestibular hypofunction. It may also be positive in polyneuropathies and dorsal column disease, but those patients do not fall consistently to one side.

Starts in nucleus ambiguus; longest peripheral course of all cranial nerves (up to splenic flexure of colon); motor to pharyngeal muscles (except stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palati), palatoglossus and larynx; smooth muscle of tracheobronchial tree, oesophagus and **GI** tract up to junction of middle and distal third of transverse colon; somatic sensation from back of ear, external auditory canal, parts of tympanic membrane, pharynx, larynx and posterior fossa dura

Spinal root supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid

blocks.note: **Q14**: acute vertigo, double vision, one-sided facial numbness, ataxia and absent gag reflex = Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome, common with posterior inferior cerebellar artery lesions - not in the notes. **Q24**: amaurosis fugax (temporary loss of vision in one eye from reduced retinal blood flow, a possible sign of impending stroke) after carotid thromboembolism is also not in the notes.

**Q10**: cerebellar dysfunction features (truncal ataxia, dysdiadochokinesia, past pointing, intention tremor; micrographia is basal ganglia/Parkinson's), **Q41**: finger-nose ataxia from inferior olivary nucleus lesions, **Q33**: absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars in subacute combined degeneration of the cord, and **Q29**: progressive supranuclear palsy (vertical gaze palsy, tau, gait unsteadiness) are tested in the bank but not covered by these notes.

blocks.text: Finger-nose ataxia = inferior olivary nucleus lesion (it supplies climbing fibres to the cerebellum; appendicular ataxia tested by the finger-nose test) - not inferior or superior colliculus, thalamus or pyramidal decussation.

A small focal lesion of one inferior olivary nucleus gives finger-nose ataxia (not right-left disorientation, visual inattention, anosognosia or oculomotor apraxia); the explanation stresses the incoordination is of the **CONTRALATERAL** arm and leg, unlike other cerebellar lesions, which cause ipsilateral dysfunction.

Absent ankle jerks **WITH** upgoing plantars = subacute combined degeneration of the cord (also seen in syphilitic taboparesis, Friedreich's ataxia and **MND**): the afferent limb of the spinal reflex is affected while **UMN** damage still gives a Babinski - a pure corticospinal/internal capsule **UMN** lesion gives exaggerated ankle reflexes/clonus instead.

Spared eye movements is the '**NOT** associated' option for progressive supranuclear palsy: early unsteady gait and falls, vertical gaze palsy (supranuclear ophthalmoplegia), dementia, brainstem (midbrain) degeneration and tau tangles are associated.

A carotid bruit with thromboembolism -> amaurosis (fugax): temporary loss of vision in one eye from reduced retinal blood flow, possibly a sign of impending stroke - not nystagmus, ataxia, transient global amnesia or diplopia.

Involuntary flinging movements of the extremities = hemiballismus (unilateral, rapid, violent flinging of the proximal arm from a lesion, usually infarct, near the contralateral subthalamic nucleus; self-limited over 6-8 weeks) - not chorea, athetosis or writer's cramp.
In normal pressure hydrocephalus, gait impairment is the symptom most likely to improve after shunting - not executive function, visuospatial deficits, cognitive impairment or urinary incontinence.
