bullets.text: CN I: only sensory nerve with no thalamic relay; unilateral anosmia = nerve/bulb/tract lesion (frontal meningioma, head injury); temporal/uncinate lesion causes none because representation is bilateral; hyposmia early in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasmal lesion; left homonymous hemianopia = right retrochiasmatic lesion; superior quadrantanopia = contralateral temporal radiation; inferior = contralateral parietal radiation; cortical blindness = occipital cortex.
Funnel vision (organic: 2 m field larger than 1 m) vs tunnel vision (no disparity; hysteria/malingering).
Cortical blindness: bilateral PCA occlusion, macular sparing/keyhole vision; may deny deficit (Anton's).
Light-near dissociation: Argyll Robertson (neurosyphilis, diabetes; Accommodation Reflex Present, light absent) and Adie (tonic pupil).

CN III: midbrain; ptosis, down-and-out eye, pupil involved; pupil-sparing in diabetes/vasculitis/MS; only ocular motor nerve causing diplopia in more than one direction. CN IV: superior oblique. CN VI: horizontal diplopia, false localising sign.
CN V: face sensation and mastication, jaw deviates to paralysed side, corneal reflex afferent V efferent VII; CN VII LMN = whole ipsilateral face, UMN = lower half only.

Weber/Rinne: conductive loss = Weber to abnormal ear, Rinne negative; sensorineural = Weber to normal ear. Romberg falls to the side of vestibular hypofunction; cold caloric nystagmus opposite, warm same (COWS).
CN IX/X: gag and palatal reflexes reduced, uvula deviates to the normal side; XI trapezius/SCM; XII tongue deviates to the paralysed side.
Finger-nose ataxia = inferior olivary nucleus; absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars = subacute combined degeneration.

blocks.text: Traumatic brain injury results from mechanical forces applied to the skull and transmitted to the brain, leading to focal and/or diffuse damage. Focal lesions often result from a direct blow and include laceration, contusion, intracerebral haemorrhage, subarachnoid or subdural haemorrhage and ischaemic infarct.

blocks.title: Concussion vs contusion
rows: Transient coma for hours followed by apparent complete clinical recovery
Prolonged coma, focal signs and lasting brain damage
Pathological support for the distinction is poor
Occurs directly beneath (coup) or contralateral (contrecoup) to the site of impact

blocks.text: Contre-coup injury is most common in the orbital-frontal area and temporal tips, where acceleration/deceleration forces drive the brain onto bony protuberances. A frontal behavioural dyscontrol syndrome occurs in bilateral orbitofrontal injury.

**Q11**: after a fall, behaviour change, violent outbursts, impulsivity and reduced fluency point to bilateral orbito-frontal contre-coup injury on **MRI** (pseudopsychopathy results from orbitofrontal damage).

Mechanisms of **TBI** include axonal and neuronal damage from direct trauma, shearing and rotational stresses on the decelerating brain, brain oedema and raised intracranial pressure, and brain hypoxia and ischaemia. Differential motion of the brain in the skull can shear and stretch axons causing diffuse axonal injury (**DAI**), which damages a more widespread area with extensive white matter tract lesions and is more often associated with persistent vegetative state and coma.

blocks.title: Post-traumatic vs retrograde amnesia after head injury
rows: Anterograde amnesia for the period of injury and the period following injury until normal memory resumes
Dense amnesia for the period between the last clearly recalled memory before injury and the injury itself
Mostly minutes; duration reduces gradually with increasing time after the injury (as written in the notes)

blocks.text: **GCS** at 24 hours after injury is widely used to assess severity. Other indices: length of coma (**LOC**), duration of **PTA**, and the Abbreviated Injury Scale (**AIS**). **LOC** and **PTA** have been used to predict functional outcome and **AIS** to predict survival; most investigations found **LOC** or **PTA** more predictive of functional status than **GCS**.

The major use of the Glasgow Coma Scale is to predict mortality (used for triage after **TBI**; **GCS** below 8 can mean a mortality rate as high as ==70%==) - its ability to predict functional outcome is not well established.

Poor prognostic factors for psychiatric morbidity after head injury: long duration of loss of consciousness, long **PTA**, elderly, chronic alcohol use, diffuse brain damage, new-onset seizures and focal damage to the dominant lobe.

blocks.title: PTA duration, severity and functional outcome
rows: May return to work in under 1 month
May return to work in 2 months
May return to work in 4 months
May require more than 1 year to return to work

blocks.title: Late sequelae of head injury
rows: Common, especially after closed head injuries with **PTA** lasting more than 24 hours
Most likely after injury to the orbitofrontal lobe or anterior temporal lobe
Depression is the most common sequela; depression and anxiety occur in roughly 1/4 of survivors; suicide risk is also higher
Headache, dizziness, insomnia, irritability, emotional lability, increased sensitivity to noise and light, fatigue, poor concentration, anxiety and depression

Schizophrenia-like psychosis with prominent paranoia with left temporal injury; affective psychoses (esp. mania, in ==9%== of patients) with right temporal or orbitofrontal injury; increased prevalence of schizophrenia (about ==2.5%== develop it)
==5%== of closed and ==30%== of open head injuries (usually in the first year); worsens prognosis
Less psychopathology after head injury due to increased brain plasticity

blocks.text: Post-concussion syndrome: processing speed is the most obviously affected neuropsychological measure - not procedural memory, block design, verbal fluency or picture matching.

bullets.text: TBI = focal (contusion, haemorrhage, infarct) and/or diffuse damage; contrecoup most common in orbital-frontal area and temporal tips; bilateral orbitofrontal injury gives frontal behavioural dyscontrol.
Concussion = transient coma with apparent full recovery; contusion = prolonged coma, focal signs, lasting damage (distinction poorly supported).
DAI (shearing of axons, widespread white matter lesions) is more often linked to persistent vegetative state and coma.
Severity indices: GCS at 24 h, LOC, PTA, AIS; LOC and PTA predict functional outcome better than GCS (AIS predicts survival).
Poor prognostic factors: long LOC, long PTA, elderly, chronic alcohol use, diffuse damage, new seizures, dominant-lobe focal damage.
PTA <60 min mild (back to work <1 month); 1-24 h moderate (2 months); 1-7 days severe (4 months); >7 days very severe (>1 year).
Depression is the most common sequela (about 1/4 with depression/anxiety); left temporal injury gives schizophrenia-like psychosis, right temporal/orbitofrontal gives affective psychosis (mania 9%).
Post-traumatic epilepsy: 5% closed, 30% open head injuries.
GCS mainly predicts mortality; post-concussion syndrome most affects processing speed.
